concept.name: Volatility smile
concept.definition: The volatility smile is the empirical pattern in which options at strikes far from the money trade at higher implied volatilities than at-the-money options of the same expiration, producing a U-shaped (or skewed) curve of implied volatility versus strike. It contradicts the constant-volatility assumption of Black-Scholes and reflects the market's pricing of fat-tailed and asymmetric return distributions.
concept.intuition: If Black-Scholes were right, every strike would imply the same volatility; instead the market charges extra for the wings, tracing a smile — the visible signature that crash and rally insurance costs more than the model says it should.
concept.mechanics: Plotting implied volatility against strike (or delta) for one expiry yields the smile/skew curve; equity markets show a downward-sloping 'skew' or 'smirk' (OTM puts bid), FX markets a more symmetric smile. The smile appeared prominently in equity index options only after the 1987 crash, as traders repriced tail risk. Smile-consistent pricing motivates stochastic-volatility (Heston), local-volatility (Dupire), and jump models.
concept.failure_modes: Interpolating or extrapolating the smile naively can imply negative probabilities or arbitrageable prices (butterfly/calendar arbitrage); smiles also morph non-parallel in stress, so hedges calibrated to one smile shape fail when the shape itself moves.
concept.misconceptions: The smile is not proof that 'the market predicts a crash' — wing implied vols embed supply, demand, and risk premia as well as probability beliefs. It is also not an arbitrage opportunity; it is the set of prices the market actually charges.
concept.example: With SPX at 5,000 and 30-day ATM implied vol at 14%, the 4,500 put might trade at 22% implied and the 5,500 call at 12% — the characteristic equity skew, one side of the smile family.
